canberra.title: Teen sentenced over ‘frightening’ attacks that ‘brutally violated’ woman and girl
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. A now-17-year-old boy has received a partially suspended six-and-a-half-year sen...
canberra.content:
One of the boy’s victims was attacked when she was walking on a trail in the Little Mulligans Flat Reserve in May 2025. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

A now-17-year-old boy has received a partially suspended six-and-a-half-year sentence for sexually assaulting one girl in Canberra’s centre and attacking a woman on a bushwalk.

The boy was 15 when he met his first victim on a night out in March, 2025. The pair’s separate groups began talking before the 17-year-old girl said she wanted to buy more alcohol.

He offered to go with her, but took her on an alternative route to the agreed bottle shop, which he claimed was a “shortcut” and the “best way to go”.

When they were in a park area, he tried to kiss her, but she said no and that she had a boyfriend.

The boy proceeded to push the girl to the ground behind a bench and sexually assault her, including choking the victim and pulling her hair, demanding “open your eyes”.

“The victim couldn’t recall how many times she was choked,” Justice Louise Taylor stated as part of her sentencing remarks on Friday (23 October).

“The victim [was] saying ‘no’ on every occasion.”

The offending lasted about half an hour. He stopped momentarily when a group of people walked past, but he prevented the girl from getting their attention.

When it was over, the boy asked the girl if she’d consented.

When she replied she hadn’t, “he began freaking out”.

The boy “started telling the victim he hadn’t raped her or touched her” and that if she contacted the police “she’d be in trouble” as she was older than him.

His second victim was attacked while he was on bail for counts of an act of indecency without consent, an act of endangering life, and sexual assault in the third degree – all charges relating to the sexual assault of the 17-year-old girl.

The 60-year-old woman was walking on the Oak Hill Trail in Little Mulligan’s Flat Reserve on 26 May 2025.

She heard someone running behind her and stepped off the trail. The then-15-year-old boy grabbed her around the neck from behind, and they both fell down; he also had his legs wrapped around the woman’s torso.

The woman lost consciousness, but came to when he loosened his grip.

She managed to free herself, but the boy grabbed her by the legs while saying “shush, just shush” and dragged her towards him.

He punched the woman in the face and grabbed her hair before sexually assaulting her. She managed to push him off, and he then grabbed her phone and ran off.

The woman ran to a stranger for help.

Police found the boy nearby and took him into custody.

He was charged with counts of indecency in the second degree, an act of indecency without consent and theft in regard to the attack on the 60-year-old woman.

During his sentencing on Friday (23 October), Justice Taylor described both attacks as “harrowing” for each victim, and examples of the types of “unpredictable, random, frightening” offending that saw women and girls move about in the world looking over their shoulders.

“He brutally violated the freedom and autonomy [of each] victim,” she stated.

Justice Taylor outlined that the boy had been diagnosed with a neurological development disorder which impacted his maturity, impulse control and communication skills, and he’d been exposed to family violence, drugs and alcohol misuse, and an unstable family environment from a young age. He had also been binge drinking and using various substances since about the age of 13.

Despite his issues, she did not accept that this significantly reduced his moral culpability.

“[He] used his physical strength to overpower each victim,” she stated.

“The signs were so obvious, that despite [his neurological issues] he could have only known, in each case, the victim was not consenting.”

Justice Taylor said the attack on the first victim “was not momentary” and he only stopped assaulting the second victim because she “managed to push [him] away”.

The pre-sentence report noted he had been “respectful and [had a] mature demeanour to staff and other people” while on remand at Bimberi Youth Justice Centre, and showed he could be “kind, considerate and caring” to others.

He had also expressed remorse for his actions, but couldn’t explain why he hurt both people.

The authors expressed concerns he could begin using alcohol and drugs if released, and there was a risk he could re-offend “under destabilising circumstances”.

Justice Taylor had to consider whether no other sentencing options were available, given the offender was under 18 and the law allows imprisonment of a young offender only as a last resort.

She determined she had no other option but to send him to prison.

Justice Taylor noted “punishment alone” wouldn’t rehabilitate the boy, but it would help change his behaviour.

“The custodial environment is operating to support his rehabilitation at a critical time,” she said.

She acknowledged the risk that the boy would be institutionalised and wouldn’t have the chance to practise his behavioural management skills in the real world.

Overall, Justice Taylor sentenced the boy to six-and-a-half years, backdated to begin on 26 May 2025, and suspended after two years.

This means he will be on a good behaviour order from 25 May 2028 to 25 November 2031.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Drink driver sent to prison for Tura Beach crash that killed friend
canberra.snippet: A drunk driver who killed his friend in a Tura Beach crash has been told to work on his issues with alcohol as an acting judge sent him t...
canberra.content:
23 October 2026

Edward James McCoid was sentenced in Bega District Court for a Tura Beach crash that killed his passenger. Photo: Albert McKnight.

A drunk driver who killed his friend in a Tura Beach crash has been told to work on his issues with alcohol as an acting judge sent him to prison.

Edward James McCoid was 33 when he chose to get behind the wheel on 21 June 2025.

The Tweed Shire man’s actions resulted in him losing control of his vehicle, causing it to veer off the road and roll.

Both McCoid and his 46-year-old male passenger were critically injured in the crash.

The older man could not be revived.

McCoid was later arrested in Queanbeyan in August and charged with dangerous driving occasioning death, drink driving and negligent driving occasioning death.

During his sentencing in Bega District Court on Friday (23 October), Acting Judge Andrew Haesler noted McCoid had a “long history of problematic alcohol use” which appeared to be a coping mechanism for his generalised anxiety disorder.

“Obviously there is a nexus between his alcohol substance abuse disorder and this offence,” he stated.

McCoid undertook two rehabilitation programs while on bail for his offending, but relapsed.

In a pre-sentence report, the author was guarded about the possibility that McCoid wouldn’t drink and drive again.

The prosecution also submitted McCoid presented an “ongoing danger” to the community if he were to receive a community-based sentence.

“The community has to be protected from him,” Acting Judge Haesler agreed.

“But he must be released [eventually] and [reducing his danger to the community] goes to his future rehabilitation.

“Everyone will benefit if he’s released to at least deal with his anxiety and [alcohol use].”

Acting Judge Haesler stated McCoid had to find a different way of managing his anxiety than drinking.

“If he cannot overcome his alcoholism, and [again] drives while intoxicated, he will be a risk,” he said.

Acting Judge Haesler sentenced McCoid to six years’ imprisonment, backdated to 27 July 2026.

He also imposed a non-parole period of three years and 10 months, making McCoid eligible for parole on 26 May 2030.

Acting Judge Haesler noted McCoid’s release on parole would be subject to the state parole authority.

But he felt if McCoid engaged in programs in custody to overcome his alcohol dependence, and showed “that you’re not a risk on release”, parole was likely.

Given McCoid pleaded guilty to his crimes, he received a two-year reduction on his sentence.

Acting Judge Haesler had this message for those who chose to drink and drive:

“They should think about the possibility of death – to them and their friends – not just that they could go to prison,” he said.

Original Article published by Claire Fenwicke on About Regional.

canberra.title: ACT moves to save bees, but there’s a sting in the tail
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has agreed to strengthen protection for bees and other pollinators across Canberra, but questions remain over funding ...
canberra.content:
The ACT Assembly has backed new measures to protect Canberra’s bees and other pollinators. Photo: Facebook.

The ACT Government has agreed to strengthen protection for bees and other pollinators across Canberra, but questions remain over funding as a destructive parasite threatens the territory’s beehives.

The Legislative Assembly backed measures to expand pollinator-friendly planting, support beekeepers and improve community education, with Greens amendments securing greater consideration of pollinators in government planning and environmental policies.

The debate came as the Varroa mite continues to spread across the ACT, affecting around half of Canberra’s estimated 6000 beehives and destroying more than 1000.

Canberra Liberals MLA Elizabeth Lee questioned the lack of dedicated funding in the recent ACT Budget to implement the government’s Nature Conservation Strategy.

“The government can produce strategies, frameworks and action plans, but without funding they remain little more than aspirations on paper,” Ms Lee said.

“If the government is serious about improving nature conservation outcomes, it must explain how these measures will be delivered without any dedicated funding.”

Responding, Environment Minister Suzanne Orr said the strategy was being finalised through cabinet processes and would be implemented over 10 years.

“At this point, for the record, we do have a lot of funding that is going towards the activities that are flagged in that strategy,” she said.

Ms Orr said existing programs were already supporting conservation work, even if the funding was not specifically listed under the strategy in the Budget. Additional investment would be considered as implementation progressed.

No new funding was announced during the debate.

The motion, introduced by Labor MLA Taimus Werner-Gibbings, called for practical measures to protect bees, butterflies, moths and other pollinators essential to biodiversity and food production.

Mr Werner-Gibbings warned that the Varroa mite, first detected in the ACT in April 2025, was expected to reach every local hive by the end of 2027.

The parasite weakens honeybees and spreads viruses, threatening colonies and potentially reducing pollination of backyard fruit and vegetable crops.

Canberra Regional Beekeepers Association president Mark Peterson said beekeepers were struggling with significant hive losses.

“We’re facing, at the moment, with the arrival of Varroa, a significant decline in the population of managed hives; there are a lot of hives just dying,” he told Region.

“Any support that we could get from the Assembly to support education and supporting research activities to address that would be gratefully received by the beekeeping community,” he added.

Mr Peterson said the association had not made a formal funding request or identified a specific amount needed. It was continuing to work with ACT Biosecurity and discussing the renewal of an agreement for access to Jerrabomberra Wetlands.

Greens MLA Jo Clay said pollinator protection needed to extend beyond individual gardens into Canberra’s parks, streetscapes and planning policies.

“We need pollinators to be factored into major planning frameworks, including our ACT Government landscape plan that is currently being developed by the government landscape architect,” she said.

Pointing to Ginninderry’s pollinator corridor project, she said thoughtful planting could provide food and habitat for bees year-round without significantly increasing costs.

Ms Orr supported the amendments, confirming the government had met with ACT for Bees and the government landscape architect to discuss incorporating pollinator protection into the developing landscape plan.

She said the review of municipal infrastructure standards would also consider suitable planting, while community garden grants had been expanded to include pollinator projects.

The government is developing educational material for residents and community groups and providing beekeepers with training and assistance through ACT Biosecurity.

Ms Orr said 95 per cent of ACT beekeepers were hobbyists. She pointed to a sentinel hive and training facility at Pialligo established to improve surveillance and early detection of biosecurity threats.

The amended motion passed with support across the Assembly, including a commitment for the government to report back on progress.

canberra.title: Mother’s alleged neglect of children resulted in serious harm
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A court has heard a Bega Valley mother is alleged to have neglected her two ...
canberra.content:
A Bega Valley woman, aged in her 30s, has been handed two charges related to child neglect. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A court has heard a Bega Valley mother is alleged to have neglected her two children so severely that her son was left with life-threatening health issues and her daughter suffered in pain from a leg injury.

The woman, who is aged in her 30s but isn’t named to protect her children’s identities, was often seen crying when she faced the NSW Local Court on Wednesday (21 October).

The court heard it was alleged she failed to seek medical attention for her two children.

It was alleged her daughter was left in ongoing pain from a serious injury to her leg. Also, while the woman’s family, medical professionals and members of the community repeatedly raised concerns about her son due to his health and appearance, she allegedly did not seek help for him either.

The court heard that as a result of the alleged neglect, the son suffered from life-threatening medical complexities.

The alleged neglect came to an end in April 2025.

The woman had been issued her charges, which were two counts of not providing for a child causing danger of serious injury, so she was originally not placed on bail.

But she didn’t go to the Bega Local Court when her matter was heard there earlier this month, resulting in a warrant being issued for her arrest.

The police prosecutor, Sergeant Perry, opposed her bail application on Wednesday (21 October), saying he was concerned about the safety of her children and the community.

Stewart Holt, the woman’s lawyer, suggested the prosecutor’s concerns should only be for the safety of the children, not the wider community.

He admitted his client didn’t go to Bega’s court earlier this month, but said that was because she had spoken to her lawyer at the time who told her she didn’t need to attend.

Mr Holt also said his client had post-traumatic stress disorder and her two children now lived with their grandmother.

“I still do everything that I’m meant to do, just with Mum,” the woman told the court when describing how she still interacted with her children.

Acting Judge Keith Alder said there was no doubt that the charges were serious. But he said the woman was now undergoing treatment for herself and her children were in their grandmother’s care.

He allowed her to be released from custody, but placed her on bail and ordered her to report to a Bega Valley police station three days a week.

The matter was adjourned to later in October at the Bega Local Court. It was not immediately clear if pleas had been entered.

canberra.title: Snowy Hydro 2.0 now set to cost up to $25 billion
canberra.snippet: A review of one of the country’s biggest infrastructure projects has found it’s expected to cost up to $25 billion. That&#821...
canberra.content:
A tunnel in the Snowy Hydro 2.0 project – now set to be fully commissioned in late 2029. Photo: Supplied.

A review of one of the country’s biggest infrastructure projects has found it’s expected to cost up to $25 billion.

That’s the finding of a “line-by-line” cost reassessment of the Snowy Hydro 2.0 project.

The review, announced last year, has found the project is now expected to cost $22.2 billion, with about $3 billion set aside as a buffer.

While the project was initially set to cost $2 billion, Snowy Hydro announced that its cost had been revised to $12 billion in 2023.

In a statement, Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said that while the finding was disappointing, the 2023 reset had limited the budget blowout.

“I have no doubt that moving from a fixed price contract, which was never suitable for such scale, uniqueness and complexity, has protected the project from an even greater cost increase,” he said.

“It’s also likely that under a fixed price contract, the project would again be stopped under the weight of billions of dollars of claims from the contractor, as it was prior to the reset.”

At the 2023 reset, it also announced the completion date was pushed out to 2028.

But the new review has pushed the finish line back by a year – to late 2029.

In its submission to a parliamentary inquiry about the project’s management, Snowy Hydro said various reasons were behind the growing price tag.

The company pointed to “design immaturity” and its “inherent complexity” (including its remote location in the Snowy Mountains) as reasons for the cost increase.

“Productivity underperformance and cost escalation have also been significant factors,” the submission outlines.

“Others have related to project-specific complexities that have developed during delivery.”

Meanwhile, principal contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) said Snowy 2.0 wasn’t immune from cost increases across the construction industry.

“The project has not been spared from these pressures and there have been further increases from the cost estimated by the parties at the reset, caused by (among other things) necessary design changes, additional adverse geological and hydrogeological conditions and significant market and labour escalation,” its submission states.

The Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) examined the 2023 contract reset in a separate report.

It found that while the 2023 reset was driven by a “largely sound approach”, project management had only been “partly effective” since.

A project benefits analysis, prepared by engineering consultant GHD, was released alongside the review’s findings.

It found the Snowy 2.0 delivery would contribute $18.3 billion to the Australian economy and lower wholesale electricity costs by more than $7 billion by 2075.

Mr Barnes said that once completed, Snowy 2.0 would have significant long-term benefits for Australia’s energy reliability.

“The scale of Snowy 2.0’s energy storage is world-leading. More than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050 will come from Snowy 2.0 alone,” he said.

“Like the original Snowy Scheme, which still underpins energy reliability more than 70 years on, Snowy 2.0 is a generational investment in our energy sovereignty and a national asset owned by all Australians.”

Once completed, the project will connect two reservoirs with underground tunnels and a new power station.

It’s expected to have a 2200 MW capacity, enough to power three million homes for a week.

According to the 2026 review, 65 per cent of tunnelling is complete, while cavern excavation is at 90 per cent.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

australia.title: Jordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlight
australia.snippet: David Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates looms Get our new p...
australia.content:
More than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon Steele-John had behaved inappropriately towards women made headlines, his position in the party remains in limbo and its new leader’s handling of the issue in question.

David Shoebridge’s first major challenge at the helm of the federal Greens came earlier this month when the Nine newspapers reported a three-page letter had been sent to him urging an independent investigation into Steele-John.

It referred to secondhand allegations that the Western Australian senator had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

As a progressive party that prides itself on taking such matters seriously and fairly, it made sense that Shoebridge announced the 32-year-old’s leave amid an independent probe into the claims.

But the process quickly became more complicated. Days later, a defiant Steele-John rejected the allegations against him, denied he agreed to take leave from parliament, and accused an internal faction within the WA Greens of playing “nasty political games” in its decision to release the letter to the media.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Steele-John said he made a public statement because he didn’t want his silence on the letter’s claims to be perceived as guilt.

While Shoebridge insists Steele-John agreed to take leave, he acknowledges he alone does not have the power to force the senator to do so.

Only if two-thirds of the party room – or more than seven members – decided to expel him in a secret ballot would Steele-John have to comply.

Such a move would be nuclear. Even if the WA Greens’ independent investigation clears him of any wrongdoing, Steele-John’s standing in the party room would be shattered.

The week ahead under scrutiny

On Monday, Shoebridge’s ability to deal with the matter will be on show.

Senate estimates is a time for members of the upper house to have their moment in the spotlight. For the Greens, it’s a chance to extricate answers about government policies from carefully trained bureaucrats to drive home a political point.

With the NDIS undergoing major changes between now and the decade’s end, the Greens will have to decide whether their disability spokesperson, Steele-John, who is championed and well-liked within the disability community, should be allowed to attend. Perhaps, virtually.

For many supporters within and outside the Greens, the optics of allowing a federal party member accused of sexual misconduct – even though a complainant has not directly come forward to make those allegations – to continue public duties will be a tough pill to swallow. Particularly as the “manosphere” phenomenon and backlash against the #MeToo movement gain momentum in mainstream society.

The question over whether the allegations were politically motivated by adversaries of Steele-John looking to gain advantage in the state’s pre-selection is a part of the equation.

But the fact remains that the rumours have persisted over the senator’s time in office. Even if they are malicious, as Steele-John contends, the simpler option would still be to stand aside and settle them while they are investigated.

The decision over whether to force Steele-John to take leave will be as much about Shoebridge’s leadership as it is about the party’s processes.

The party room, and its membership more broadly, prides itself on being a movement based on consensus decision-making.

Shoebridge will need the support of the party room to take the expulsion route. How he handles this issue will also set the tone for the rest of his leadership and, depending on his actions, could prompt an ugly battle with Steele-John.

It’s a quagmire – politically, legally and ethically.

There are unlikely to be any winners.

australia.title: Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse
australia.snippet: High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries Get our new political email , ...
australia.content:
Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.

Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.

In other words, things are getting worse, not better.

Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.

Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.

The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.

Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month.

That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles.

Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.

Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.

With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.

High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.

It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.

“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.

“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.

“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”

The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.

Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.

But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.

His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”

Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.

Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?

This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.

australia.title: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows
australia.snippet: Trial results represent ‘foundational shift’ in approach to cancer, allowing scientists to harness immune system in more personalised way...
australia.content:
A personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years, new clinical trial results show.

The vaccine, intismeran, is custom-made to target genetic mutations unique to an individual’s melanoma. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III clinical trial.

The Australian-led trial included 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but were at high risk of it returning.

All were treated with an immunotherapy drug called pembrolizumab for twelve months, and some were also given the personalised intismeran vaccine.

The trial found that at two years post treatment, the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with treatment with pembrolizumab alone.

Prof Georgina Long, medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia and 2024 Australian of the Year, described the findings as “a foundational shift in our approach to cancer”, allowing scientists to “harness … the immune system in a more personalised way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development.”

Long will present the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual congress in Madrid on the weekend.

The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and will need to go through a process of peer review.

Patients in the trial – conducted across 157 sites worldwide – had not previously received any cancer drug treatment. Of those receiving the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab, 82% were alive and recurrence-free after two years, compared with 70% of participants treated with pembrolizumab alone.

In a phase III trial, a treatment is tested in a large group of people and compared with standard treatments; it is necessary before drug regulators can approve a medicine for use in the general population.

In recent years, developments in immunotherapy drugs have significantly increased survival rates for people with advanced melanoma.

Dr Jessamy Tiffen, acting deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Innovations at the Centenary Institute, who was not involved in the research, said what was “truly remarkable” about the vaccine was the “deeply personalised nature of the treatment, something cancer researchers have been striving to achieve for decades”.

“Where previously oncologists could pick a targeted therapy based on a single gene mutation present in the melanoma, this bespoke mRNA vaccine targets up to 34 gene mutations, unique to each patient. This vaccine, in combination with another type of immunotherapy, then trains the immune system to recognise and eliminate the melanoma, and most importantly, stop it from coming back.”

She noted that the treatment, if progressed, would not benefit all people with melanoma. “A significant portion do not respond to the vaccine in the first instance,” she said.

“Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them. Only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years, but the results are clear that the combination works better than immunotherapy alone, and that’s a very exciting development.”

The drug manufacturers said it was too early to tell from the data whether the combination treatment improved long-term survival.

Prof Christopher Sweeney, director of the South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute at Adelaide University, described the vaccine as “a step-change approach for how to improve the body’s immune system to see cancer cells as foreign and then augment the ability to prevent the cancer cells growing and recurring”.

He said more research was needed to see if the approach was effective in patients “who have cancer we can see”, or who were not responsive to the immune enhancer pembrolizumab.

The personalised vaccine will not be available as a standard melanoma treatment until it has gone through further study and regulatory review, a process that may take several years.

australia.title: Decomposing whale near Sydney’s Coogee beach should be towed out to sea, Indigenous rangers say
australia.snippet: The juvenile humpback carcass is wedged between rocks and attracting sharks, but is too decayed to be moved for burial Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
A First Nations ranger group says a whale carcass that closed two of Sydney’s most popular beaches after washing up this week should be towed out to allow it to decompose in the ocean.

Coogee beach reopened on Friday after closing on Thursday, when a whale carcass, believed to be a juvenile humpback, was found washed up in Lurline Bay, between Coogee and Maroubra beaches. Randwick city council confirmed the reopening on Friday but said Maroubra beach remained closed due to “dangerous surf conditions”.

But the council said the carcass remained wedged among rocks after high tide had failed to move it out to sea as hoped.

“People should avoid Lurline Bay and not swim or enter the water in the immediate area. The area remains barricaded off,” the council said.

They said a drone flyover on Thursday evening had not spotted any shark activity, so lifeguards decided Coogee was safe to reopen. Swimmers were urged to swim between the flags.

But they added that high tide on Friday evening could move the carcass closer to the water’s edge one again, potentially attracting sharks.

The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people. Robert Cooley, a senior ranger at the Gamay Rangers, who have been working with the council on a culturally respectful way to deal with the remains, said the tide had pushed the carcass higher up towards a coastal walkway, requiring an intervention.

“The preferred option now is to tow it back out to sea.” he told Guardian Australia ahead of an afternoon briefing with the council.

“Now that it’s up there and decaying and several vertebrate and other bits of bone are showing, people have a habit of taking collections home, which is quite distressing to us.”

The Gamay Rangers undertake natural and cultural resource management activities like protection work, conservation, and threatened species management in the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council area.

Cooley said that because the whale was in an advanced stage of decay, it was too challenging to lay it to rest on conservation land owned by the land council, as a young humpback that washed up on Cronulla beach earlier this year had been.

“It’s just a big pile of blubber now, but the priority is to let nature take its course [out at sea]. The second priority would be lay it to rest on our conservation land.”

He said the Gamay Rangers did not support taking the whale to landfill.

“It’s really distressing to know that a significant ancestor of ours is taken to landfill with the rest of the city’s rubbish.”

Concerns were raised earlier this year about the towing of a sperm whale carcass along a 20km stretch of coast south of Sydney to Wollongong before being taking it to landfill, resulting in increased shark activity and catching swimmers off guard.

Olaf Meynecke, manager of the whales and climate research program at Griffith University, has been involved two successful whale tows this year in New South Wales and one in Queensland.

He said taking whale carcasses to landfill was “unethical, and … not very environmentally friendly”, towing them far out to sea, typically to the start of the continental shelf – up to 50km offshore – allowed them to decompose naturally and support the marine environment, including sharks.

“We actually do want the sharks to bite into these carcasses because it helps to decompose it quickly,” he said.

“It’s actually a pretty good thing because then you get rid of the sharks from the nearshore areas where people are bathing.”

He said while explosives had been used in the past to break up whale carcasses onshore, now they were typically only used while towing to “open up one side of the whale so that the decomposition will happen a lot faster”.

“The only thing that keeps the whale buoyant is is the intestines and the methane that’s being created through gut bacteria.

“Once that compartment is opened and the guts release all the methane, the whale will start sinking.”

In Western Australia this week, the popular Cottesloe beach was closed amid fears of shark activity due to a three-metre decomposed partial whale carcass.

The Cottesloe mayor, Melissa Hawkins, told the ABC the council had organised a bulldozer to take the remains to landfill.

With whale migration season in full swing, the ABC reported that watchers in Jervis Bay off the NSW south coast were greeted by the a rare sighting of an orca pod, believed to be hunting a humpback.

australia.title: Nationals leader Matt Canavan eyes move to lower house as pollster warns of One Nation wipeout
australia.snippet: Michelle Landry announces she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia at the next election Get our new political email , fr...
australia.content:
Matt Canavan could attempt a switch to the House of Representatives after a colleague announced her looming retirement, as a leading pollster said the Nationals leader had a “zero per cent” chance of holding his Senate seat if the One Nation polling surge remains unchanged.

Veteran National MP Michelle Landry on Friday announced she would not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia, around Rockhampton, at the next election.

Responding to speculation that Pauline Hanson could attempt her own switch to run in that seat, Landry said One Nation was “not very pleasant” and criticised the party’s “obnoxious” cartoon videos.

“I think they need to pull their heads in,” Landry said of One Nation.

There has been heavy speculation Canavan will run in Capricornia. Canavan earlier this month said he would do “whatever it takes” to hold Capricornia, telling Sky News: “if I’m required, if it is required to keep a seat, to hold one more seat in the lower house somewhere. I will do it.”

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

On Friday, at a press conference with Landry, Canavan shrugged off questions but did not rule it out. Landry denied she was pushed to resign from Capricornia to make way for another Nationals member, and declined to speculate on who could run as her replacement.

The Coalition leader, Angus Taylor, also declined to speculate about a Canavan lower house switch when asked at a separate press conference, only praising the Nationals leader as an “extraordinary colleague”.

Kos Samaras, director at polling group Redbridge, said Canavan faced losing his Senate spot in 2028, pointing to current polling showing a One Nation surge which he claimed could see Hanson’s party win upper house seats currently held by the Coalition.

Senators up for re-election in Queensland at the next poll include two LNP members in James McGrath and Canavan, two Labor, one Greens, and Hanson herself. But One Nation’s surge means the party could win one or more additional Senate seats, most likely at the expense of the second person on the LNP ticket – Canavan.

“He goes from a 0% chance of being elected as a senator, to potentially winning [in Capricornia],” Samaras said.

“That will also be difficult, because of One Nation, but he [Canavan] is in a better position going downstairs.”

Last month’s Guardian Essential poll showed One Nation with a 25% primary vote nationwide, with Labor at 29% and the Coalition at an all-time low 22%.

Landry took a parting shot at One Nation, and the prospects if Hanson were to attempt a run in Capricornia, in her press conference.

“I’ve had a lot of dealings with One Nation over the years, and I can tell you, most of it hasn’t been very pleasant.

“When I look at people that move into an area to run for a political position, it doesn’t usually end well,” Landry said.

Samaras pointed to Redbridge polling showing what he called “a complete wipeout” of the Coalition at the hands of One Nation, specifically a large analysis from May showing Hanson’s party winning up to 59 seats nationally – largely from the Liberals and Nationals.

“On current polling, they’ll win nearly every seat the LNP holds in Queensland,” Samaras said, including Senate spots.

“If there’s a state in this country that’s good for One Nation, it’s Queensland.”

However, Samaras noted large “volatility” in polling nationwide, noting that the Queensland’s state LNP government was polling well.

“Things can change,” he said.

world.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
world.snippet: 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’ Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record Lewis Hamilton has said h...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

world.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
world.snippet: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’ The US-backed hepat...
world.content:
The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

world.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
world.snippet: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail Send us your questions ...
world.content:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday-night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, in a statement to the Guardian late on Wednesday, said it was “a false story designed to smear the brave men and women of ICE as they are facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them”.

“No sick detainees are being deported. All detainees are medically cleared before travel and leave with any necessary medications.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said her husband has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

The DHS statement said Sendra was “a criminal illegal alien from Cuba convicted of fraud, larceny, and property crimes” and “has been consistently cleared and discharged from the hospital following medical evaluation”.

He was ordered removed from the US in September 2015, it said.

“Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets,” the spokesperson said.

“Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal, and the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe.”

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

world.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
world.snippet: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its c...
world.content:
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

world.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine resear...
world.content:
Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.

Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.

“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.

The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.
